title: CSC2400 Module 3: Divide and Conquer — Matrix Multiplication

questions.q: X and Y are n × n matrices and Z = X · Y. Which formula gives entry Z_ij?
questions.explain: Take row i of X and column j of Y, multiply matching pairs, and add them up. The shared index k is the column index in X and the row index in Y.

questions.q: Entry Z_ij of Z = X · Y is computed from the i-th column of X and the j-th row of Y.
questions.explain: It is the reverse: the i-th ROW of X and the j-th COLUMN of Y. The row comes from the left matrix and the column from the right matrix.

questions.q: X = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and Y = [[5, 6], [7, 8]] (rows listed top to bottom). What is entry Z_21 of Z = X · Y?
questions.explain: Row 2 of X is (3, 4) and column 1 of Y is (5, 7). 3·5 + 4·7 = 15 + 28 = 43. The full product is [[19, 22], [43, 50]].

questions.q: X = [[2, 0], [1, 3]] and Y = [[4, 1], [2, 5]] (rows listed top to bottom). What is entry Z_22 of Z = X · Y?
questions.explain: Row 2 of X is (1, 3) and column 2 of Y is (1, 5). 1·1 + 3·5 = 1 + 15 = 16. The full product is [[8, 2], [10, 16]].

questions.q: X = [[a, b], [c, d]] and Y = [[e, f], [g, h]]. What is the bottom-left entry Z_21 of X · Y?
questions.explain: Row 2 of X is (c, d) and column 1 of Y is (e, g), so Z_21 = ce + dg. The full product is [[ae + bg, af + bh], [ce + dg, cf + dh]].

questions.q: How many scalar multiplications does the ordinary row-times-column formula use to multiply two 2 × 2 matrices?
questions.explain: There are 4 entries and each needs 2 multiplications (for example Z_11 = ae + bg), so 4 × 2 = 8.

questions.q: X and Y are both 10 × 10. How many scalar multiplications does it take to compute ONE entry Z_ij of X · Y with the row-times-column formula?
questions.explain: One entry is a sum of n products X_ik · Y_kj for k = 1..n. With n = 10, that is 10 multiplications (and about as many additions).

questions.q: In the standard triple-loop algorithm (loops i, j, k with Z[i][j] += X[i][k] * Y[k][j] inside), what does the innermost k loop do?
choices: Chooses which row of Z is being filled
Walks along row i of X and down column j of Y, building the sum for the single entry Z[i][j]
Chooses which column of Z is being filled
Adds the finished entries of Z together to form the result
questions.explain: The i loop picks the row, the j loop picks the column, and the k loop accumulates X[i][k] · Y[k][j] over k = 1..n to compute one entry.

questions.q: What is the running time of the standard triple-loop matrix multiplication algorithm for n × n matrices?
questions.explain: Each of the three nested loops runs n times, so the innermost statement runs n · n · n = n³ times.

questions.q: The standard triple-loop algorithm multiplies two 10 × 10 matrices. How many times does the innermost statement Z[i][j] += X[i][k] * Y[k][j] execute?
questions.explain: The loops run n, n, and n times, so the inner statement runs n³ = 10³ = 1000 times.

questions.q: Which is a correct way to explain why the standard algorithm takes Θ(n³) time?
choices: There are n entries in Z, and each takes about n² work
There are n³ entries in Z, and each takes constant work
There are n² entries in Z, and each takes about n multiplications and additions
There are n² entries in Z, and each takes constant work
questions.explain: Z is n × n, so it has n² entries. Each entry is a sum of n products, so the total is n² × n = n³.

questions.q: In Divide and Conquer matrix multiplication, X is split into blocks A, B, C, D and Y into blocks E, F, G, H. What size is each block?
questions.explain: Each matrix is cut into four quarters (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right). Each quarter has side length n/2.

questions.q: What key observation makes recursive (Divide and Conquer) matrix multiplication possible?
choices: Block matrices multiply exactly like 2 × 2 matrices of numbers, with the blocks in place of the numbers
Matrix multiplication is commutative, so the blocks can be multiplied in any order
Each entry of the product depends on only one block of X
The product of two blocks is always a 1 × 1 matrix
questions.explain: XY = [[AE + BG, AF + BH], [CE + DG, CF + DH]] has the same shape as the 2 × 2 formula. Each block product is a smaller copy of the original problem, so it can be solved recursively.

questions.q: X = [[A, B], [C, D]] and Y = [[E, F], [G, H]], where each letter is a block. Write the top-right block of XY (use the block letters, e.g. "PQ + RS").
questions.explain: Top-right = (top row of X) times (right column of Y) = AF + BH.

questions.q: X = [[A, B], [C, D]] and Y = [[E, F], [G, H]] are block matrices. What is the bottom-left block of XY?
questions.explain: Bottom-left = (bottom row of X) times (left column of Y) = CE + DG. EC + GD has the factors reversed. Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so the X-block must stay on the left.

questions.q: In the block formula for XY, the product AE can be written as EA, since swapping the factors gives the same result.
questions.explain: Blocks are matrices, and matrix multiplication is not commutative. The X-block always goes on the left: AE, not EA.

questions.q: How many recursive matrix multiplications does the straightforward Divide and Conquer algorithm make at each level?
questions.explain: AE, BG, AF, BH, CE, DG, CF, DH. Each multiplies two (n/2) × (n/2) matrices.

questions.q: X = [[A, B], [C, D]] and Y = [[E, F], [G, H]]. Which of these block products does straightforward Divide and Conquer compute?
questions.explain: The eight products are AE, BG, AF, BH, CE, DG, CF, DH. EA has the factors reversed. BE and AG do not appear in any block of XY.

questions.q: After the eight recursive products are computed, how many (n/2) × (n/2) matrix additions does straightforward Divide and Conquer need to build the four result blocks?
questions.explain: Each result block is the sum of two products (AE + BG, AF + BH, CE + DG, CF + DH), so that is one addition per block, 4 in total.

questions.q: The base case of Divide and Conquer matrix multiplication is reached when the matrices are 1 × 1. If X = [x] and Y = [y], the algorithm returns [xy].
questions.explain: A 1 × 1 matrix cannot be split further, so the algorithm just does one scalar multiplication.

questions.q: Which recurrence describes straightforward Divide and Conquer matrix multiplication?
questions.explain: There are 8 recursive multiplications, each on (n/2) × (n/2) matrices, plus Θ(n²) work to split and to do the 4 block additions. T(1) = Θ(1).

questions.q: In the recurrence T(n) = 8T(n/2) + Θ(n²) for Divide and Conquer matrix multiplication, what does the Θ(n²) term represent?
choices: The cost of the eight recursive multiplications
The cost of the 1 × 1 base case
The number of levels of recursion
The non-recursive work: splitting the matrices and the block additions that combine the products
questions.explain: Adding two (n/2) × (n/2) blocks touches n²/4 entries. A constant number of such additions, plus the split, is Θ(n²).

questions.q: Each matrix is cut into 4 blocks. Why is each subproblem T(n/2) and not T(n/4)?
choices: Each block has side length n/2, and n is the side length of the matrices
Because 8 subproblems divided by 4 blocks gives 2
Because only half of the blocks are used in each product
Because the base case is 2 × 2 rather than 1 × 1
questions.explain: n measures the side length. A quarter of an n × n matrix is (n/2) × (n/2), so each subproblem has size n/2.

questions.q: What is the asymptotic running time of straightforward Divide and Conquer matrix multiplication (8 recursive multiplications)?
questions.explain: Solving T(n) = 8T(n/2) + Θ(n²) with the Master Method gives Θ(n³), the same as the triple loop. Divide and Conquer only reorganizes the same work.

questions.q: Splitting a problem into smaller subproblems with Divide and Conquer always improves its asymptotic running time.
questions.explain: Plain Divide and Conquer matrix multiplication splits the problem and is still Θ(n³). The improvement only comes from reducing the number of subproblems, as Strassen does.

questions.q: Plain Divide and Conquer reaches the 1 × 1 base case after log₂ n levels and makes 8^(log₂ n) base-case multiplications. What does 8^(log₂ n) simplify to?
questions.explain: 8^(log₂ n) = n^(log₂ 8) = n³. That is exactly the number of scalar multiplications the triple loop does.

questions.q: For n = 4, how many base-case scalar multiplications does plain Divide and Conquer (8 recursive calls per level) perform?
questions.explain: There are log₂ 4 = 2 levels, so 8² = 64 = 4³.

questions.q: For n = 16, how many base-case scalar multiplications does Strassen's algorithm (7 recursive calls per level) perform?
questions.explain: There are log₂ 16 = 4 levels, so 7⁴ = 2401. Plain Divide and Conquer would do 8⁴ = 4096 = 16³.

questions.q: Using the same split into four (n/2) × (n/2) blocks, what has to change to beat Θ(n³)?
choices: Make the base case 2 × 2 instead of 1 × 1
Reduce the number of recursive multiplications
Recurse on the blocks in a different order
questions.explain: The number of recursive calls ends up in the exponent: n^(log₂ a). Going from a = 8 to a = 7 changes n³ into about n^2.807. The base case, the order of the calls, and the Θ(n²) additions do not change the exponent.

questions.q: How many recursive matrix multiplications does Strassen's algorithm make at each level?
questions.explain: Strassen computes seven products P1 through P7, one recursive multiplication each, instead of the eight in plain Divide and Conquer.

questions.q: Using X = [[A, B], [C, D]] and Y = [[E, F], [G, H]], which of these is Strassen's P1?
questions.explain: P1 = A(F − H). The others are P2 = (A + B)H, P4 = D(G − E), and P7 = (A − C)(E + F).

questions.q: Using X = [[A, B], [C, D]] and Y = [[E, F], [G, H]], which of these is Strassen's P5?
questions.explain: P5 = (A + D)(E + H): the diagonal of X times the diagonal of Y. P6 = (B − D)(G + H) and P7 = (A − C)(E + F). (A + B)(E + G) is not one of Strassen's products.

questions.q: Which of these is Strassen's P4?
questions.explain: P4 = D(G − E). (C + D)E is P3. D(E − G) has the subtraction the wrong way round, which would flip the sign of P4.

questions.q: In Strassen's algorithm, which combination gives the top-right result block C12?
questions.explain: C12 = P1 + P2 = (AF − AH) + (AH + BH) = AF + BH, which matches the block formula.

questions.q: In Strassen's algorithm, which combination gives the bottom-left result block C21?
questions.explain: C21 = P3 + P4 = (CE + DE) + (DG − DE) = CE + DG, which matches the block formula.

questions.q: In Strassen's algorithm, which combination gives the top-left result block C11?
questions.explain: C11 = P5 + P4 − P2 + P6. Only P2 is subtracted. Expanding it gives AE + BG. P1 + P5 − P3 − P7 is C22.

questions.q: In Strassen's formula for the bottom-right result block C22, which products are SUBTRACTED?
questions.explain: C22 = P1 + P5 − P3 − P7. P1 and P5 are added, and P3 and P7 are subtracted.

questions.q: Expand Strassen's P2 = (A + B)H, keeping the order of the matrix factors.
questions.explain: (A + B)H = AH + BH. H stays on the right because matrix multiplication is not commutative, so HA + HB is wrong.

questions.q: In Strassen's formulas C11 = P5 + P4 − P2 + P6, etc., what does C11 refer to?
choices: Block C of X (the bottom-left block)
The top-left entry of block C
The top-left block of the result XY
questions.explain: C11, C12, C21, C22 are the blocks of the result. The letter C is also used for the bottom-left block of X, but those are different things.

questions.q: Each Strassen product P_i costs exactly one recursive matrix multiplication. The sums and differences inside the parentheses are computed first and are not multiplications.
questions.explain: For example, P5 = (A + D)(E + H) does two additions and then one recursive multiplication.

questions.q: Treat each entry of X = [[2, 0], [1, 3]] and Y = [[4, 1], [2, 5]] as a 1 × 1 block: A = 2, B = 0, C = 1, D = 3, E = 4, F = 1, G = 2, H = 5. What is P5 = (A + D)(E + H)?
With A = 2, B = 0, C = 1, D = 3, E = 4, F = 1, G = 2, H = 5, what is P6 = (B − D)(G + H)?
For X = [[2, 0], [1, 3]] and Y = [[4, 1], [2, 5]], Strassen's products include P2 = 10, P4 = −6, P5 = 45, P6 = −21. What is C11?
For X = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and Y = [[5, 6], [7, 8]], Strassen's products include P1 = −2, P3 = 35, P5 = 65, P7 = −22. What is C22?
What is the asymptotic running time of Strassen's algorithm?
questions.explain: The recurrence T(n) = 7T(n/2) + Θ(n²) solves to Θ(n^(log₂ 7)) ≈ O(n^2.807), which is asymptotically better than O(n³).

questions.q: Strassen's algorithm runs in Θ(n^x). Give x to three decimal places.
Compared with straightforward Divide and Conquer, Strassen's algorithm does fewer matrix additions and subtractions at each level.
questions.explain: Strassen does fewer recursive MULTIPLICATIONS (7 instead of 8) but MORE additions and subtractions: 18 instead of 4.

questions.q: How many matrix additions must be done before the recursive multiplication in Strassen's P5 = (A + D)(E + H)?
questions.explain: A + D and E + H. Compare P1 = A(F − H), which needs one subtraction.

questions.q: Count the block additions and subtractions in one level of Strassen's algorithm: those needed to form P1 through P7, plus those needed to combine them into C11, C12, C21, C22. What is the total?
questions.explain: Forming the products takes 10 (one each for P1 to P4, two each for P5 to P7). Combining takes 8 (3 for C11, 1 for C12, 1 for C21, 3 for C22). 10 + 8 = 18.

questions.q: Strassen does many more block additions and subtractions than plain Divide and Conquer. Why doesn't this hurt its asymptotic running time?
choices: Additions are only done at the 1 × 1 base case
The extra additions and subtractions cancel each other out
There is a constant number of them, each Θ(n²), so the non-recursive work per call is still Θ(n²)
Additions take Θ(1) time no matter how large the blocks are
questions.explain: Each block addition is Θ(n²) work, and 18 is a constant, so the combine work is still Θ(n²), the same order as plain Divide and Conquer. Only the number of recursive calls (7 vs. 8) changes the exponent.

questions.q: Why does cutting the number of recursive multiplications from 8 to just 7 change the asymptotic running time?
choices: The saving is repeated at every level of the recursion, so the number of calls ends up in the exponent: n^(log₂ 8) = n³ vs. n^(log₂ 7)
It saves one-eighth of the work at the top level, which is a big enough constant factor
Strassen also halves the number of matrix additions
Seven subproblems make the recursion shallower than eight
questions.explain: Saving one multiplication at a single level would only be a constant-factor gain. Because each of the 7 subproblems also uses 7 calls, and so on, the base-case count is 7^(log₂ n) = n^(log₂ 7) instead of n³.

questions.q: Which general algorithm-design idea does Strassen's algorithm illustrate?
choices: Always split a problem into as many subproblems as possible
Sometimes you can spend more time on one part of an algorithm to greatly reduce the cost of another part
Any recursive algorithm is faster than an iterative one
Minimizing additions is the key to fast matrix multiplication
questions.explain: Strassen takes on extra Θ(n²) addition and subtraction work in exchange for fewer recursive multiplications, and that improves the overall exponent.
